record.title: BenchShield models agent-evaluation reward integrity across the full task lifecycle
record.summary: A September 10 arXiv paper presents BenchShield, which models reward-relevant events in interactive agent benchmarks and combines static phase-aware taint analysis with runtime evidence from the evaluation infrastructure. The authors report a corpus of 456 human-adjudicated trajectories selected from more than 31,000 public runs across Terminal-Bench 3, SkillsBench and ClawsBench. On paired, author-selected task audits, reported full-chain exploit recall rises over an agentic scanner baseline in all three benchmark sets (for example, 0.77 vs 0.23 on Terminal-Bench 3 and 1.00 vs 0.94 on ClawsBench, union over five trials). Runtime attribution reports 96% accuracy among covered cases in 144 runnable cells, with 87.5% coverage and inconclusive verdicts for the rest. Results are author-reported and do not establish general benchmark prevalence, complete exploit prevention or transfer to unrelated environments.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper specifies a finite reward-relevant lifecycle model and combines static phase-aware taint analysis with runtime evaluation-infrastructure evidence to distinguish exposed exploit paths from observed agent use.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report 456 human-adjudicated trajectories selected from more than 31,000 public runs spanning Terminal-Bench 3, SkillsBench and ClawsBench; 314 of the 456 selected trajectories contain adjudicated reward-hacking episodes. This selected corpus fraction is not a prevalence estimate for all 31,000 source runs.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On paired task audits, the paper reports improved full-chain recall over BenchJack in each evaluated benchmark set, with union-over-five-trials values of 0.88 vs 0.25 on SkillsBench, 1.00 vs 0.94 on ClawsBench, and 0.77 vs 0.23 on Terminal-Bench 3.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the runtime attribution study, BenchShield reports 96.0% accuracy among covered cells across 144 runnable cases, with 87.5% coverage; 18 cells are inconclusive, and the paper reports 36 additional cells that could not exist or launch because of task-package limitations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The evaluation uses Claude Opus 5 for model calls and author-defined adjudication on three benchmark families; it does not establish performance on arbitrary or production agent environments.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction was located or performed; evaluation and trajectory labels come from the authors’ selected benchmark/task set and adjudication protocol.
The lifecycle specification may omit reward-relevant infrastructure paths, and the study does not establish completeness against adaptive agents that know the instrumentation.

Runtime accuracy is reported among covered cases and class balance is task-selected; 18 of 144 runnable cells are inconclusive. Performance at deployment base rates and fixed false-positive budgets is unknown.

The 456 reviewed trajectories are selected from more than 31,000 public runs and include benchmark-specific adjudication; the 69% selected-corpus fraction does not estimate general reward-hacking prevalence.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported instrumentation generalizes, reward-hacking evidence could become a reusable, infrastructure-backed property of agent evaluations instead of a collection of task-specific patches. This could materially change how capability and safety programs establish score integrity. The result is major rather than field-shifting because it is an author-run evaluation across three benchmark families with a finite declared lifecycle model, and independent transfer and adaptive-attack testing are absent.
limitations: All implementation and performance results are from the author-run evaluation; the research desk did not execute the artifact or reproduce the study.
The 456 trajectories are a selected, adjudicated corpus; 314/456 is not the prevalence of reward hacking among all 31,000+ source runs.
Runtime 96% accuracy applies among covered runnable cells only; 87.5% coverage and inconclusive cases are material.
Three benchmark families do not represent all reward mechanisms, external side effects, distributed infrastructure or real production agents.
A declared finite lifecycle model can miss paths the task binding omits; adaptive evasion is not established as solved.
Benchmark reward integrity is distinct from whether a benchmark validly measures real-world capability.
brief.summary: A September 10 arXiv paper presents BenchShield, which models reward-relevant events in interactive agent benchmarks and combines static phase-aware taint analysis with runtime evidence from the evaluation infrastructure. The authors report a corpus of 456 human-adjudicated trajectories selected from more than 31,000 public runs across Terminal-Bench 3, SkillsBench and ClawsBench. On paired, author-selected task audits, reported full-chain exploit recall rises over an agentic scanner baseline in all three benchmark sets (for example, 0.77 vs 0.23 on Terminal-Bench 3 and 1.00 vs 0.94 on ClawsBench, union over five trials). Runtime attribution reports 96% accuracy among covered cases in 144 runnable cells, with 87.5% coverage and inconclusive verdicts for the rest. Results are author-reported and do not establish general benchmark prevalence, complete exploit prevention or transfer to unrelated environments.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report a 456-trajectory adjudicated corpus, improved full-chain recall over BenchJack in three benchmark families, and 96% runtime attribution accuracy among covered runnable cells. The 96% figure is accuracy, not recall, and the study reports 87.5% verdict coverage.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv v1 report documents the lifecycle model, annotation protocol, task bindings, infrastructure evidence, experimental tables and limitations. the research desk inspected the full HTML sections and tables but did not execute the repository, reproduce annotations, or independently rerun the evaluation.
technical.mechanism: The paper models the lifecycle from task packaging and agent-visible state through tool actions, verifier inputs, artifact handling and reward collection. Static phase-aware taint checks inspect possible paths before execution; runtime instrumentation seals infrastructure-side events and uses structural plus semantic evidence to issue a verdict or abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting.
technical.novelty: Treats evaluation integrity as a lifecycle and provenance problem spanning agent-visible state, hidden state, outcome construction and reward collection, then combines static path discovery with runtime host-side evidence and explicit inconclusive verdicts.
technical.regime: 189 task instances across 96 unique upstream tasks and three benchmark families; static paired audit results use repeated trials on adjudicated exploit chains. Runtime attribution uses 180 labeled cells, of which 144 were runnable. Model calls in the study use Claude Opus 5 with high reasoning effort.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint provides a detailed protocol and reports artifact/repository material; the research desk did not inspect or run the code and no independent reproduction was located in this review.
technical.strongest_baseline: BenchJack agentic hackability scanner on the same pinned task packages and model for static discovery; transcript-only LLM attribution is separately reported at 36% accuracy in the runtime study appendix.

brief.title: BenchShield models agent-evaluation reward integrity across the full task lifecycle
brief.why_it_matters: Agent benchmark scores depend on a chain of environment state, agent actions, verifier inputs and reward collection. The paper offers a concrete way to model and audit that chain using host-side evidence rather than relying only on the agent transcript or a post-hoc language-model judge. If the reported results generalize, evaluation infrastructure could provide stronger evidence that a score came from an intended task path. The finite lifecycle model and selected benchmark set leave coverage of real systems and adaptive attacks open.
